e-9577.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14062909/assets/0f4f0de23892a6f76642f8c7e5d3a6112a8ffa2d9f50000cd974f293a7d8b3b6.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
e-9577.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(0,-1)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-0)^2 + (y - (-1))^2 = 2^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + (y+1)^2 = 4.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

e-9578.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to an Ellipse
e-9578.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14062909/assets/d3895bafe045f7e460887aee41bf390fdda753fed87eaab14f4a29ddb792267c.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
e-9578.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $2$ and $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{4^2} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}) & =0 \\ \frac{2x}{4}+\frac{2y}{16}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

e-9579.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parabola
e-9579.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14062909/assets/a92eae1ab0af29ea895b570c95199ece1e292c09953ebb2dabbb7c6e2d422d6c.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the right-opening parabola shown above.
e-9579.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(3,-2).$

The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
y^2 = 4px.
$$

Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)^{2} & =4p(3) \\ 4 & =12p \\ p & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
y^2 = \dfrac{4}{3}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{3}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(-1,1)$ and has a radius of $1,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-(-1))^{2}+(y-1)^{2}={1}^{2}\,⟹\,(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y-1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x+1)+2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x+1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{y-1} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+1}{1-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
content.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(-1,1)$ and has a radius of $1,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-(-1))^{2}+(y-1)^{2}={1}^{2}\,⟹\,(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y-1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x+1)+2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x+1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{y-1} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+1}{1-y}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(-3,-2)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-(-3))^{2}+(y-(-2))^{2}={2}^{2}\,⟹\,(x+3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=4.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+3)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+2)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x+3)+2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x+3) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
content.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at the origin and has a radius of $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={4}^{2}\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(16) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x-1)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x-1)+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
after.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $3$ and $1,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{2x}{9}+2y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x}{9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{9y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
after.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at $(3,0)$ and has semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{(y-0)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{9})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{2(x-3)}{9}+\frac{2y}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2(x-3)}{9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4(x-3)}{9y}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(-1,2).$

The general equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ and $y=2$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{2} & =4p(-1) \\ 4 & =-4p \\ p & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
{y}^{2}=-4x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2}{y}\end{aligned}
$$
